extracted.intended_audience: military lawyers, judge advocates, commanding officers, and others applying or interpreting the Articles of War
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and precedent-focused exposition of what kinds of acts fall within particular Articles of War (sixtieth, sixty-first, sixty-second, etc.), and how to treat jurisdiction, elements, and sentencing/mitigation questions in courts-martial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commander's discretion to refer homicide to civil authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a Philippine scout killed another scout under circumstances which the department commander believed amounted to murder, it was within the department commander's discretion to turn him over to civil authorities without bringing him to trial before a general court-martial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such referral to civil jurisdiction does not contravene Army Regulations (970 of 1910); the department commander's reasonable belief that the act amounted to murder supports waiver of military jurisdiction (C. 21694, July 9, 1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicating pay accounts equals presenting fraudulent claim
rubrics_metrics.description: The offense known as duplicating of pay accounts, where it generally involves presenting or causing to be presented a false or fraudulent claim against the United States, is properly chargeable under the relevant article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duplicating a 'pay account' is treated as causing a false/fraudulent claim against the government (cases cited: B. 37, 356, Feb., 1876; 42, 569, Mar., 1880; C. 14619, Aug. 14, 1903; 16131, Apr. 5, 1904).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collusion with contractor and false vouchers is offense
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer who, by collusion with a contractor, received less supply than the United States was entitled to but issued a voucher certifying delivery of the whole amount, is chargeable with the offense defined in the article's 8th paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misrepresenting delivery to conceal receipt of pecuniary consideration from contractor constitutes the specified offense (R. 35, 206, Feb., 1876).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using government property for private benefit = misappropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: When an officer used teams, tools, and other public property in his possession as such officer to erect buildings etc. for the benefit of a mainly civilian association of which he was a member, he was properly chargeable with misappropriation of United States property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loaning or using government property for private purposes is an offense even if local practice exists; such practice, unless properly sanctioned by superior authority, is no defense though sanction may be shown in mitigation of sentence (R. 10, 664, Dec., 1864; R. 29, 26, June, 1869; R. 29, 189, Aug., 1869).

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary personal use of government horses = applying property to own use
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a quartermaster used temporarily, with his private carriage, a pair of Government horses in his charge, he was not chargeable with embezzlement but with the offense of knowingly applying to his own use and benefit property of the United States furnished for the military service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes embezzlement from 'applying to his own use' — the latter is still an offense under the Article (R. 4, 421, Dec., 1863).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to transfer/disburse public moneys is prima facie embezzlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 5495 R.S. provides that refusal by any person charged with disbursement of public moneys promptly to transfer or disburse funds upon legal requirement shall be deemed prima facie evidence of embezzlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in military cases: if a disbursing officer refuses to turn over public moneys when legally required, burden shifts to him to show his proceedings were justified; prosecution need not show what became of the funds (R. 22, 548, Jan., 1867).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inducing fraudulent leases to obtain allowance of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an officer willfully induced another to make to the United States a lease containing false and fraudulent statements for the purpose of obtaining allowance of a fraudulent claim, he was chargeable with the specified offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such inducement to procure fraudulent claims falls within the fourth paragraph's class of offenses (P. 132, 189, July, 1890).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forgery of discharge/final papers to procure pay is offense
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier who forged the name of his commanding officer on discharge and 'final statement' papers and presented them to a paymaster was chargeable with offenses defined in the relevant paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forgeries to procure improper discharge/pay are chargeable under multiple paragraphs (R. 28, 668, June, 1869).

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsifying military records (e.g., clothing book) is an offense
rubrics_metrics.description: Falsifying an entry in a company clothing book constitutes an offense under the sixtieth article of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific record falsifications (rolls, returns, vouchers, books) have been held to be offenses (C. 17555, Feb. 16, 1905).

rubrics_metrics.name: Larceny of property furnished/intended for military service
rubrics_metrics.description: The offense of stealing as indicated in the ninth paragraph consists in larceny of 'property of the United States furnished or intended for the military service.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except in time of war, larceny of other property can be charged as a military offense only when it prejudices good order and military discipline (see Sixty-second article).

rubrics_metrics.name: Misappropriation need not be for personal profit
rubrics_metrics.description: The misappropriation specified in the article need not be an appropriation for the personal profit of the accused; 'to his own use or benefit' qualifies only the term 'applies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conviction may be for applying public property to unauthorized uses even absent personal profit (R. 23, 77, June, 1866).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution after discharge/dismissal permitted within limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the concluding provision of the article, a soldier may be brought to trial for specified offenses while held imprisoned after dishonorable discharge for another offense, provided the statute-of-limitations (two years under article 103) has not expired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law supports trial of discharged personnel for prior offenses within statutory limit (R. 31, 344, Nov., 1870; other cases listed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman'
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct need not be 'scandalous and infamous' nor directly connected to military service; it is sufficient that it is morally wrong, disgraceful or disreputable, manifests unfitness both as an officer and a gentleman, and compels dismissal in all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slightly discreditable acts are ordinarily not charged; the conduct must show the party unworthy to hold a commission (R. 2, 52, Mar., 1863; C. 17667, Mar. 18, 1900). Examples provided in subsequent subparagraphs clarify scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: False official reports/certificates are 'unbecoming' conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowingly making to a superior a false official report, or deliberately false official certificates as to vouchers, rolls, returns, etc., is chargeable under the 'conduct unbecoming' article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately false official statements of material character have been held offenses (R. 1, 365, Oct., 1862; R. 27, 290, Oct., 1868; R. 42, 585, Apr., 1880; C. 23277 cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: False accusations, subornation, corrupt inducement, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Preferring false accusations against an officer; attempting to induce an officer to join in a fraud upon the United States; attempt at subornation of perjury are offenses within the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated as specific kinds of 'conduct unbecoming' (R. 27, 435, Dec., 1868; R. 38, 671, July, 1877).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal misuse of government hospital supplies
rubrics_metrics.description: A surgeon appropriating food furnished by the Government for hospital patients to his own private mess is guilty of an offense under the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriation of supplies intended for patients is a clear example of offense (R. 2, 33, Feb., 1863).

rubrics_metrics.name: Violations of promises of honor to superiors are punishable
rubrics_metrics.description: Violation by an officer of a promise or pledge on honor given to a superior (e.g., abstain from intoxicating drink) is chargeable under the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breaking honorable pledges made to secure withdrawal of charges has been held an offense (R. 27, 297, Oct., 1868; C. 22394, Jan. 14, 1908).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disorderly public conduct in uniform (drunkenness, fights) is offense
rubrics_metrics.description: Appearing in uniform drunk and conducting oneself disorderly in public, engaging in fights when intoxicated, or violent public altercations in sight of officers and soldiers are offenses under the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include drunk in uniform at theatre attracting attention (R. 25, 479, Apr., 1868; 38, 140, July, 1876) and fights at public places or billiard rooms (R. 42, 445? Jan., 1880; R. 27, 635, Apr., 1869).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gambling with enlisted men or visiting disreputable houses in uniform
rubrics_metrics.description: Gambling with enlisted men in public or visiting a disreputable gambling house in uniform and gambling are offenses within the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conduct in presence of soldiers/civilians has been held to constitute an offense (R. 37, 127, Mar., 1873; R. 42, 633, May, 1880).

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect of pecuniary obligations may be 'dishonorable' conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere neglect to satisfy private pecuniary obligations will not ordinarily furnish sufficient ground for charges, but where debt was dishonorably incurred (false promises) or nonpayment accompanied by fraud/deceit/denial, continued nonpayment may constitute an offense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases establish when indebtedness becomes dishonorable and thus chargeable; repeated complaints, indifference, or failures after assurances can aggravate to offense status (R. 13, 425, Feb., 1865; R. 23, 564, July, 1867; many cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Using checks representing nonexistent funds can be an offense
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an officer, in payment of a debt, gave his check on a bank representing he had funds when in fact he had none and was aware of it, he was amenable to a charge under the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation of funds when none exist may be considered dishonest conduct and chargeable (R. 13, 207, Jan., 1865).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bigamy, abandonment, abuse, neglect to support spouse/children are offenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage in contravention of existing lawful marriage (bigamy), abusing/assaulting/beating wife, failure to support wife and children without adequate cause, and instituting fraudulent divorce proceedings with manufactured testimony have been held 'conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific family-related misconduct is explicitly chargeable (R. 23, 164, Aug., 1866; R. 31, 400, May, 1871; R. 43, 21, Oct., 1879; P. 59 cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication of pay account is always offense
rubrics_metrics.description: Duplication of a 'pay account' or claim for monthly pay is always an offense under the article; it is no defense that transfer was made before pay was actually due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing regulation-based technical defense would permit taking advantage of wrongful/fraudulent act; duplication is an offense regardless (P. 50, 43, Oct., 1891; C. 25078, June 9, 1909).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Crimes' in Article 62 defined and limits on capital crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'crimes' means military offenses of more serious character, including civil crimes (homicide, robbery, arson, larceny, etc.). Capital crimes (murder or other capital-by-statute offenses) cannot be taken cognizance of by courts-martial under this article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If specification/proof shows the crime was murder and capital, the court should refuse jurisdiction; proceedings otherwise are unauthorized and void (multiple cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation: crimes must prejudice good order and military discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'to the prejudice of good order and military discipline' qualifies 'crimes' and 'disorders' — crimes are chargeable when they clearly affect order and discipline (e.g., larceny from fellow soldier or officer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include manslaughter of a soldier, assault with intent to kill a fellow soldier, forgeries affecting military finance, embezzlement of military property; non-capital crimes that prejudice discipline are within scope (many cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of criticism of fellow officers is unmilitary
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer printing/publishing to the Army a criticism upon an official report of another officer, or publishing charges/insinuations in a newspaper that asperse a fellow officer's character, is gravely unmilitary conduct to the prejudice of good order and military discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officer should prefer charges or appeal for redress rather than public publication; publication calls for serious punishment even if published charges are true (R. 39, 431, Feb., 1878; R. 42, 284, May, 1879).

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegal withdrawal/application of public funds by disbursing officer = embezzlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Withdrawing public funds from an authorized depository for a purpose not prescribed or authorized by law (personal use or to pay claims not due) is properly charged as embezzlement under statute (sec. 5488 R.S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory embezzlement is a form of the sixty-second article; intent (fraudulent or not) is immaterial to the statutory crime though may mitigate punishment. Restoration of funds before formal demand is no defense (R. 25, 588; R. 33, 291; others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Embezzlement: receipt of public money and failure to account
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer who, in his official capacity, receives public money (not pay or allowance) and fails duly to account for it to the United States is guilty of embezzlement; statute makes no distinction as to source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual conversion, motive, or destination of funds is immaterial for statutory offense; failing to pay into Treasury or account for moneys exacted from contractors is embezzlement (P. 52, 138, Feb., 1892).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized payment from proceeds of public sale is embezzlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing and paying out, from public funds (e.g., proceeds of sale of condemned quartermaster stores), an unauthorized percentage (e.g., 10%) to an enlisted man as compensation constituted embezzlement of public money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payments not authorized by law, even if for services, can constitute embezzlement (P. 59, 201, Apr., 1893).

rubrics_metrics.name: Offenses against civilians depend on circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether acts committed against civilians are offenses within the Article is determined case-by-case: e.g., if committed on military reservation or in its neighborhood (constructive presence), or by military custodians affecting military service, they may be within military jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No general rule; jurisdiction and chargeability depend on facts — location, connection to military service, and prejudice to discipline are relevant (discussion at LXII C 5 a.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between statutory embezzlement (sec. 5488) and other embezzlement
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory embezzlement of June 14, 1866 (sec. 5488 R.S.) — withdrawal/application of public funds not authorized by law — is broader and does not require fraudulent intent, and has been generally tried under the sixty-second article rather than the sixtieth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The act provides a measure of punishment and treats intent as immaterial; courts and War Department have often preferred charging under the statutory embezzlement provisions when applicable (extensive case law and G.C.M.O. citations).
